title: Fate or effort
hookLine: only the weak blame fate, Lakshmana says, and then he has to decide what to do with his strength
carry: fate and effort, daiva and purushakara, both count

lines: HOW MUCH IS UP TO US?
cards: A few days ago, Rama told Lakshmana not to blame Kaikeyi: what had happened was daiva, larger than any one person. It's a gentle idea, and Lakshmana hates it.
He stands with his brow knotted, and Valmiki says he's breathing hard, like an angry snake in its hole.
He answers with an argument people have quoted ever since, the other side of an old question: how much is fate, and how much is up to us?

teach.h: ONLY THE WEAK TALK OF FATE.
teach.b: Here is Lakshmana's case. Fate is what weak people talk about. A real hero pushes fate aside with his own effort.
Call this fate, and you've given up before you've tried.
Then he holds up his arms. These aren't for decoration. They're for protecting you.
Today the people will see which is stronger, fate or me. Let me take the kingdom for you. It's a powerful speech, and Valmiki doesn't make it foolish.

teach.h: ONE CHARIOT, TWO WHEELS: FATE AND EFFORT.
teach.b: In Hindu thought, effort, purushakara, is honored as seriously as fate, daiva. An old Sanskrit saying puts them together: a chariot doesn't move on one wheel.
So Rama and Lakshmana are the tradition's two voices, and you can still hear both at a Hindu dinner table: a grandmother saying it was in your fate, a parent saying work harder. But watch Rama.
He doesn't argue the philosophy again. He wipes away Lakshmana's tears and speaks to him as a brother. Know that I'm determined to keep our father's word.
Stand with me in this. And Lakshmana listens, head lowered, still grieving, still angry, and silent. This is the restraint.

teach.h: THE RAGE STAYS; HE DOESN'T SPEND IT.
teach.b: He doesn't stop feeling the rage; he chooses not to spend it. He has the arms, the bow and the courage. What he gives his brother is the hardest effort a strong person can make: holding back.
And at once the energy has somewhere to go.
If you're going to the forest, Lakshmana says, then so am I.

how: Hindu teachers often set Rama's speech on daiva, fate, beside Lakshmana's speech on purushakara, human effort, and leave listeners to weigh both.

o: a warrior's vow to avenge a wrong done
the fate the gods hand each person at birth
human effort, the old partner and rival of fate

games.q: fate or effort — tap the pairs.
p: only the weak talk of fate

s: Valmiki makes Lakshmana's argument look foolish
he gives it full force; effort is honored in Hindu thought too.
Rama answers by debating fate again
he wipes Lakshmana's tears and asks him to stand with him.
Lakshmana ends by deciding to go to the forest
if you're going, he says, so am I.

games.q: you're Lakshmana. you have the strength to take the throne for your brother, and he's asked you to stand with him instead. what do you do?
o: take it anyway; he'll thank you later.
lower your head, hold back, and go with him.
go home and stay out of it.
games.why: he falls silent, still grieving and angry, and turns his strength to following Rama into exile.

practice: Close your hands into loose fists, and feel your own strength in them for a few breaths. Then slowly open them, palms up on your knees, and notice that the strength is still there.
Breathe with them open; holding back isn't the same as being weak.

wordCard.voice: Purushakara, human effort, the old partner and rival of fate. Lakshmana argues that heroes push fate aside, then lowers his head, keeps his strength unspent, and chooses to go with Rama.

orig.note: Sanskrit puruṣakāra: human effort, what a person does; the old partner and rival of daiva, fate.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: fate and effort, daiva and purushakara, both count. And the strongest effort can be holding back. Day five hundred twenty-nine, done.
